Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)

- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# gron

Make JSON greppable!

gron transforms JSON into discrete assignments to make it easier to `grep` for what you want and see the absolute 'path' to it.
It eases the exploration of APIs that return large blobs of JSON but have terrible documentation.

## Example

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=1" | fgrep "commit.author"
json[0].commit.author = {};
json[0].commit.author.date = "2016-07-02T10:51:21Z";
json[0].commit.author.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
json[0].commit.author.name = "Tom Hudson";
```

gron can work backwards too, enabling you to turn your filtered data back into JSON:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=1" | fgrep "commit.author" | gron --ungron
[
  {
    "commit": {
      "author": {
        "date": "2016-07-02T10:51:21Z",
        "email": "mail@tomnomnom.com",
        "name": "Tom Hudson"
      }
    }
  }
]
```

## Usage

Get JSON from a file:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json 
json = {};
json.contact = {};
json.contact.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
json.contact.twitter = "@TomNomNom";
json.github = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/";
json.likes = [];
json.likes[0] = "code";
json.likes[1] = "cheese";
json.likes[2] = "meat";
json.name = "Tom";
```

From a URL:

```
▶ gron http://headers.jsontest.com/
json = {};
json.Host = "headers.jsontest.com";
json["User-Agent"] = "gron/0.1";
json["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"] = "6917a823919477919dbc1523584ba25d/11970839830843610056";
```

Or from `stdin`:

```
▶ curl -s http://headers.jsontest.com/ | gron
json = {};
json.Accept = "*/*";
json.Host = "headers.jsontest.com";
json["User-Agent"] = "curl/7.43.0";
json["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"] = "c70f7bf26661c67d0b9f2cde6f295319/13941186890243645147";
```

Grep for something and easily see the path to it:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep twitter
json.contact.twitter = "@TomNomNom";
```

gron makes diffing JSON easy too:

```
▶ diff <(gron two.json) <(gron two-b.json)
3c3
< json.contact.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
---
> json.contact.email = "contact@tomnomnom.com";
```

The output of `gron` is valid JavaScript:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json > tmp.js
▶ echo "console.log(json);" >> tmp.js
▶ nodejs tmp.js
{ contact: { email: 'mail@tomnomnom.com', twitter: '@TomNomNom' },
  github: 'https://github.com/tomnomnom/',
  likes: [ 'code', 'cheese', 'meat' ],
  name: 'Tom' }
```

It's also possible to obtain the `gron` output as JSON stream via the `--json` switch:

```
▶ curl -s http://headers.jsontest.com/ | gron --json
[[],{}]
[["Accept"],"*/*"]
[["Host"],"headers.jsontest.com"]
[["User-Agent"],"curl/7.43.0"]
[["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"],"c70f7bf26661c67d0b9f2cde6f295319/13941186890243645147"]
```

## ungronning

gron can also turn its output back into JSON:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | gron -u
{
  "contact": {
    "email": "mail@tomnomnom.com",
    "twitter": "@TomNomNom"
  },
  "github": "https://github.com/tomnomnom/",
  "likes": [
    "code",
    "cheese",
    "meat"
  ],
  "name": "Tom"
}
```

This means you can use gron with `grep` and other tools to modify JSON:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | gron --ungron
{
  "likes": [
    "code",
    "cheese",
    "meat"
  ]
}
```

Or with JSON stream mode:

```
▶ gron --json testdata/two.json | grep likes | gron --json --ungron
{
  "likes": [
    "code",
    "cheese",
    "meat"
  ]
}
```

To preserve array keys, arrays are padded with `null` when values are missing:

```
▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | grep -v cheese
json.likes = [];
json.likes[0] = "code";
json.likes[2] = "meat";

▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | grep -v cheese | gron --ungron
{
  "likes": [
    "code",
    null,
    "meat"
  ]
}
```

## Command-line Options

```
Transform JSON (from a file, URL, or stdin) into discrete assignments to make it greppable

Usage:
  gron [OPTIONS] [FILE|URL|-]

Options:
  -u, --ungron     Reverse the operation (turn assignments back into JSON)
  -v, --values     Print just the values of provided assignments
  -c, --colorize   Colorize output (default on tty)
  -m, --monochrome Monochrome (don't colorize output)
  -s, --stream     Treat each line of input as a separate JSON object
  -k, --insecure   Disable certificate validation
  -j, --json       Represent gron data as JSON stream
      --no-sort    Don't sort output (faster)
      --version    Print version information

Exit Codes:
  0	OK
  1	Failed to open file
  2	Failed to read input
  3	Failed to form statements
  4	Failed to fetch URL
  5	Failed to parse statements
  6	Failed to encode JSON

Examples:
  gron /tmp/apiresponse.json
  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 
  curl -s http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | gron
  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | grep company | gron --ungron
```

## Aliases

It's recommended that you alias `ungron` or `norg` (or both!) to `gron --ungron`:

```bash
alias norg="gron --ungron"
alias ungron="gron --ungron"
```

# Advanced Usage Examples

Although gron's primary purpose is API discovery, when combined with other tools like `grep` it can do some interesting things.

## Examples from the GitHub API

Get the last 5 commits from a repository:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5"
json = [];
json[0] = {};
json[0].author = {};
json[0].author.avatar_url = "https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/58276?v=3";
...
```

Extract just the first commit using `fgrep "json[0]"`:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]"
json[0] = {};
json[0].author = {};
json[0].author.avatar_url = "https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/58276?v=3";
...
```

Get just the committer's name and the commit message:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)"
json[0].commit.committer.name = "Tom Hudson";
json[0].commit.message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog";
```

Turn the result back into JSON using `gron --ungron`:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | gron --ungron
[
  {
    "commit": {
      "committer": {
        "name": "Tom Hudson"
      },
      "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog"
    }
  }
]
```

## Flattening Objects

gron preserves the location of values in the JSON, but you can use `sed` to remove keys from the path to flatten objects:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g"
json[0].name = "Tom Hudson";
json[0].message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog"
```

With those keys removed, the result is a 'flattened' object:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | gron --ungron
[
  {
    "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog",
    "name": "Tom Hudson"
  }
]
```

Process all commits by removing the filter:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | gron --ungron
[
  {
    "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog",
    "name": "Tom Hudson"
  },
  {
    "message": "Refactors natural sort to actually work + be more readable",
    "name": "Tom Hudson"
  },
  ...
]
```

## Including Nested Data

To include nested data like parent commit URLs:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message|parents.*html_url)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g"
json[0].name = "Tom Hudson";
json[0].message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog";
json[0].parents[0].html_url = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/gron/commit/48aba5325ece087ae24ab72684851cbe77ce8311";
...
```

Remove the `.html_url` part of the path to simplify the structure:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message|parents.*html_url)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | sed -r "s/\.html_url//"
json[0].name = "Tom Hudson";
json[0].message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog";
json[0].parents[0] = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/gron/commit/48aba5325ece087ae24ab72684851cbe77ce8311";
...
```

Convert back to JSON:

```
▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message|parents.*html_url)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | sed -r "s/\.html_url//" | gron --ungron
[
  {
    "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog",
    "name": "Tom Hudson",
    "parents": [
      "https://github.com/tomnomnom/gron/commit/48aba5325ece087ae24ab72684851cbe77ce8311"
    ]
  },
  ...
]
```
Transform JSON (from a file, URL, or stdin) into discrete assignments to make it greppable

Usage:
  gron [OPTIONS] [FILE|URL|-]

Options:
  -u, --ungron     Reverse the operation (turn assignments back into JSON)
  -v, --values     Print just the values of provided assignments
  -c, --colorize   Colorize output (default on tty)
  -m, --monochrome Monochrome (don't colorize output)
  -s, --stream     Treat each line of input as a separate JSON object
  -k, --insecure   Disable certificate validation
  -x, --proxy      Set proxy configuration
      --noproxy    Comma-separated list of hosts for which not to use a proxy, if one is specified.
  -j, --json       Represent gron data as JSON stream
      --no-sort    Don't sort output (faster)
      --version    Print version information

Exit Codes:
  0	OK
  1	Failed to open file
  2	Failed to read input
  3	Failed to form statements
  4	Failed to fetch URL
  5	Failed to parse statements
  6	Failed to encode JSON

Examples:
  gron /tmp/apiresponse.json
  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 
  curl -s http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | gron
  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | grep company | gron --ungron
gron version dev
---
json = {};
json.a = 1;
json.b = [];
json.b[0] = 2;
json.b[1] = 3;
---json
[[],{}]
[["a"],1]
[["b"],[]]
[["b",0],2]
[["b",1],3]
---values
--- ungron
{
  "a": 1
}
--- color test

[34;1mjson[0;22m.[34;1ma[0;22m = [31m1[0m;
</output>

echo "=== -s with empty line? ==="
printf '{"a":1}\n\n{"b":2}\n' | ./executable -s 2>&1; echo exit:$?
printf '{"a":1}\n   \n{"b":2}\n' | ./executable -s 2>&1; echo exit:$?

echo "=== -s with -j ==="
printf '{"a":1}\n{"b":2}\n' | ./executable -s -j

echo "=== -s with -u? shouldn't work, but test ==="
printf '{"a":1}\n{"b":2}\n' | ./executable -s | ./executable -u --stream 2>&1; echo exit:$?

echo "=== gron | gron -u ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable | ./executable -u

echo "=== gron color | gron -u? Should handle color stripping? ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable --colorize | ./executable --ungron
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable --colorize | ./executable --ungron --colorize | od -c

echo "=== json colorize handling for ungron? ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable -j -c | ./executable -j -u | od -c

echo "=== stream file with json input containing array ==="

echo "=== ungron with array holes complex ==="
printf 'json = [];\njson[0] = {};\njson[0].a = 1;\njson[1] = {};\n' | ./executable -u

echo "=== identifier detection more ==="
echo '{"valid":1,"_valid":1,"$valid":1,"a1":1,"1invalid":1,"a-b":1,"a b":1,"a.b":1,"":1}' | ./executable

echo "=== quoting of keys - check if $ is considered bare? ==="
echo '{"$":1}' | ./executable
echo '{"_":1}' | ./executable
echo '{"a$":1}' | ./executable
echo '{"a_":1}' | ./executable

echo "=== monochrome json ==="

echo "=== values for json: should not exist but test - maybe returns whole json values? ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable --json --values 2>&1; echo exit:$?
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable -j -v 2>&1; echo exit:$?

echo "=== file reading error handling for dir ==="

echo '{"b":1,"a":2}' | ./executable --json
echo '{"b":1,"a":2}' | ./executable --json --no-sort

printf '{"a":"\u0001"}' | ./executable --json

# file containing {"z":1,"a":2} order

import json
# Check if Go preserves order via custom ordered map
# Our tests show --no-sort respects input order? Let's check earlier:
# echo '{"z":1,"a":2,"m":3}' | ./executable --no-sort gave original order (z,a,m) yes.

print('{"z":1,"a":{"y":2,"x":1}}')

echo '[{"a":1},{"b":2}]' | ./executable --json

echo '{"a":1,"a":2}' | ./executable

echo "=== gron --values with file? ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable --values | cat -A

printf 'json.a = 1;\njson.b = "hello world";\n' | ./executable --values --json 2>&1; echo exit:$?

echo "=== check -v + -j + -u combined order ==="

printf '[[],{}]\n[["a"],1]\n' | ./executable -j -u -v | od -c

echo "=== -c -m both set? last wins? ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable -c -m | head

printf 'json.a = 1;\n' | ./executable -u --colorize | od -c

echo "=== check natural sort implementation details - maybe numeric sort? ==="

# We observed a1, a10, a2 order for lex sort earlier: that's lex order would be a1, a10, a2 indeed lex sorts that way. Natural would be a1, a2, a10.
# So earlier test: {"a10":1,"a2":2,"a1":3} sorted gave a1, a10, a2 -> lexicographic
# So it's lexicographic sort, not natural.

echo "=== check sorting for numbers in array indices: numeric sort naturally? ==="

printf 'json.b = [];\njson.b[10] = 1;\njson.b[2] = 2;\n' | ./executable -u

echo '{"a": "line\nbreak"}' | ./executable
echo '{"a": "\t"}' | ./executable

echo '{"a": "<script>"}' | ./executable
echo '{"a": "<script>"}' | ./executable --json

python3 <<'PY'
import json, sys

PY
python3 -c "import json; print(json.dumps({'a':'\x01'}))" | ./executable
python3 -c "import json; print(json.dumps({'a':'\x01'}))" | ./executable -j

echo '{"a":true,"b":null,"c":1,"d":"s","e":[],"f":{}}' | ./executable -c | od -c
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable -j -c | od -c

echo '1' | ./executable -j -c | od -c

printf 'json.a = {"b":1};\n' | ./executable -u -c 2>&1 | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = [1,2];\n' | ./executable -u -c 2>&1 | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = true;\n' | ./executable -u -c 2>&1 | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = null;\n' | ./executable -u -c 2>&1 | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'

printf 'json.a = 1;\n' | ./executable -v -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g' -A 2
printf 'json.a = 1;\n' | ./executable -v -c | od -c

echo "=== more sorting details ==="
echo '{"b":1,"a":2}' | ./executable

echo '{"b":2,"a":1}' | ./executable

./executable /tmp/complex2.json

echo '{"b":2,"a":1,"c":3}' | ./executable -j --no-sort

echo '{"b":{"d":4,"c":3},"a":{"b":2,"a":1}}' | ./executable -j

# Let's check behavior for stream + no-sort
printf '{"b":2,"a":1}\n{"d":4,"c":3}\n' | ./executable -s -j --no-sort

# Deep test: how does no-sort preserve order of object keys? Input order preservation should be via ordered map.
# In Go, standard json.Unmarshal loses order, so no-sort must use custom decoder that preserves order (maybe using json.RawMessage or preserving insertion order via slice)
# We already saw it does preserve input order.

# Test values mode: does it preserve sorted order? Let's see
echo '{"b":2,"a":1}' | ./executable | ./executable -u -v
echo '{"b":2,"a":1}' | ./executable --no-sort | ./executable -u -v

printf 'json.b = 2;\njson.a = 1;\n' | ./executable -u -v

# Also test -v with json stream input?

"}

printf 'json.a = 1;\n' | ./executable -u -c | cat -A | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'

printf 'json.a = false;\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = null;\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = "hi";\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = "a b";\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json = [];\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json = {};\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json[0] = 1;\njson[1] = 2;\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
printf 'json.a = {};\njson.a.b = 1;\n' | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
# more
echo '{"a":1,"b":"hi","c":true,"d":null,"e":[],"f":{}}' | ./executable -u -c 2>&1 | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g' || echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'

echo '{"a":1,"b":"hi","c":true,"d":null,"e":[1,2],"f":{"x":1}}' | ./executable | ./executable -u -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'

echo "=== json stream color ungron ==="

echo "=== gron json stream color ==="
echo '{"a":1,"b":true,"c":null,"d":"hi","e":[1]}' | ./executable -j -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'

echo "=== gron text color more ==="
echo '{"a":1}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a":true}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a":null}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a":"hi"}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a":[]}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a":{}}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a": [1,2]}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a-b":1}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '{"a": {"b-c": 1}}' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
echo '[1,2]' | ./executable -c | sed $'s/\x1b/<ESC>/g'
"}

python3 <<'PY'
# Now we see that for these cases, ungron and values actually work correctly when we properly escape via python raw strings.
# So earlier confusion was due to shell escaping.

# So string with semicolon inside is handled correctly.

# Good.

# Now we have enough to implement.

# Let's summarize the remaining unknowns for implementation:

# 1. Flag parsing with Go flag package should match error messages and help.

# 2. Color detection.

# 3. Input reading (file, URL, stdin) and error codes.

# 4. JSON parsing with order preservation and raw number preservation.

# 5. Statement generation for gron text and json stream, with sorting / no-sort.

# 6. Ungron text parsing:

#   - For -u: split by lines, ignore lines that are empty or start with space, error for lines starting with tab? Let's formalize:

# From our tests, for -u:

#   - Empty line: ignored
#   - Spaces only line: ignored
#   - Tab only line: error "ungron failed for ``: invalid statement"
#   - Line starting with space: ignored
#   - Line starting with tab: error empty
#   - Line starting with non-space, non-tab:
#       Find first ';'
#       If not found: error "ungron failed for `<line>`: statement has no value" where <line> is the whole line (without trailing newline)
#       If found: stmt = line[:index_of_;] + ';' ??? Actually includes ';'
#         Then parse stmt.

#   - For parsing stmt: should be "<path> = <value>;" with optional spaces.

#   - If after trimming, stmt is just ";" (i.e., path empty), then error empty.

#   - If path part missing or invalid, error "invalid statement"

#   - If value part missing or invalid, various errors.

#   Let's formalize parsing of statement string (including semicolon):

#   - StatementStr is trimmed? For -u, we should not trim leading spaces because leading spaces already cause ignore, but for non-space-starting lines, there may be trailing spaces. Our earlier test: "json.a = 1;   \n" parsed successfully, trailing spaces after semicolon ignored (because we only take up to first semicolon). So after finding first semicolon, we take substring up to and including semicolon, ignoring rest.

#   - That substring may have trailing spaces before semicolon? Actually "json.a = 1 ;" has space before semicolon, but semicolon is after space, so statement includes that space. That's allowed.

#   - For parsing, we need to split into path and value by "=".

#   - Find first "="? What if value contains "=" inside string? e.g., json.a = "a=b"; -> value contains "=". So we should find "=" that is outside string? Or first "="? For simplicity, we can find "=" not inside string? But typical statement has only one "=" separating path and value, and value may contain "=" inside string, but that "=" would be inside quotes. So we need to handle.

#   The simplest: Split by "=" first occurrence that is outside quotes? However for gron output, path never contains "=" and value is JSON which may contain "=" inside string, but "=" inside string should not be considered separator. So we need to find "=" outside string.

#   Similarly for semicolon, we already found first semicolon, but what if semicolon inside string? We should find semicolon that is outside string? For text statements, value is JSON primitive or {} or [] – none contain semicolon except string may contain semicolon inside quotes, which should NOT terminate statement. So we need to find semicolon outside string.

#   So parsing must handle JSON string quoting and escaping.

#   Approach: Scan statement char by char, tracking whether inside string, and handling escapes.

#   For path/value split, we need to find "=" outside string.

#   For line splitting into statement, we need to find ";" outside string.
